title: Checkpoint: Deep Time
objective: After this level you can explain how geologists read rocks, fossils and radioactive clocks to tell Earth's 4.5-billion-year story.
summary: To date a fossil, put the layers in order, date volcanic ash above and below, and match index fossils worldwide. That is how deep time got its numbers.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: date a fossil that can't be dated.
cards.body: A trilobite shell has no useful radioactive clock inside. But the rock around it might. Put this chapter's tools together and you can pin it in time, somewhere between 520 and 545 million years ago.

cards.headline: Step one: put it in order
cards.body: Start with the cliff. Superposition says that in undisturbed layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest on top. Cross-cutting says anything that slices through layers, like a dike, is younger than they are. Now you know the order of events, but not yet the years.

cards.headline: Step two: find the clocks
cards.body: Most fossils can't be dated with radioactive clocks. Volcanic ash can: its crystals grew from molten rock, so their clocks started when they formed. Date an ash layer below the fossils and another above, and the fossils are pinned between them. In one example, trilobites came out older than 520 million years but younger than 545 million.

cards.headline: Step three: match it worldwide
cards.body: If those trilobites belong to a short-lived, widespread index species, every layer that holds them anywhere in the world gets the same age range. Dates like these, gathered from rocks around the world, built the geologic time scale for a planet about 4.54 billion years old.

mascot.line: That's Levels 32, 33 and 34 as one team: order the layers, match the fossils, read the clocks.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How geologists put rock layers in order and then pin real dates on them.
Why Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and why meteorites hold the proof.
What index fossils and radioactive clocks each add to the geologic time scale.
How microbes, drifting continents and buried swamps left their marks in rock.

questions.prompt: Why do geologists date the volcanic ash around a fossil instead of the fossil itself?

options.label: Ash is softer and much easier to dig up than fossils
Fossils are always younger than every ash layer nearby
options.rationale: The ash below is older than the fossils.

options.label: Its crystals grew from molten rock and carry a clock
Fossils carry too much uranium to give a clear date
options.rationale: Fossils mostly have no usable radioactive clock of their own.

questions.explanation: Ash crystals formed from molten rock, so their radioactive clocks started when they formed; most fossils can't be dated directly.

questions.prompt: Ash below a fossil bed is 545 million years old and ash above it is 520 million. How old are the fossils?

options.label: Older than 545 million years
options.rationale: The fossils sit above the older ash.

options.label: Younger than 520 million years
options.rationale: The fossils sit below the younger ash.

options.label: Exactly 532.5 million years, the midpoint
options.rationale: The ash gives a range, not an exact midpoint.

questions.explanation: The fossils lie between the two ash layers, so their age falls between the two dates.

questions.prompt: Put the steps Hutton read in Siccar Point's cliff in order.
questions.explanation: The vertical layers were laid flat first, then tilted up, worn down and buried again under the red sandstone.

questions.prompt: How did early oxygen-making microbes leave a record in the rocks?

options.label: Their bodies piled up in swamps and turned into coal seams
options.rationale: Coal came from land plants much later.

options.label: Their oxygen rusted dissolved iron into banded iron formations
They carved long tunnels and caves through limestone
options.rationale: That isn't how they left their mark.

options.label: They filled the rocks around them with carbon-14
options.rationale: Carbon-14 is far too short-lived to last that long.

questions.explanation: Oxygen combined with iron dissolved in seawater and settled as red iron-oxide bands.

questions.prompt: What raises coal from lignite to anthracite?

options.label: More time spent drying out in the sun
options.rationale: Coal forms buried, away from sunlight.

options.label: Being washed over and over by ocean waves
Mixing with layers of volcanic ash
More heat and pressure from deeper burial

questions.explanation: Deeper burial brings more heat and pressure, which raises coal's rank and carbon content.
